beats.caption: HBM stacks feed the GPU, and every bit is charge on a capacitor
beats.text: The HBM stacks beside an AI accelerator are DRAM: each bit is a small charge on a capacitor of a few femtofarads, gated by one transistor. That charge does not stay put forever.

beats.caption: Right after a write, each cell holds full charge
beats.text: A write or refresh pushes the capacitor to a full 1 or empties it to 0. The sense amp can tell them apart as long as the stored charge stays well above the halfway point.

beats.caption: Charge leaks away; retention time is how long a bit survives
beats.text: Leakage through the access transistor and the junction drains the capacitor. Retention time is how long a cell keeps a readable charge. Most cells last seconds, but the weakest few set the rule: every row must be refreshed within about 64 ms.

beats.caption: Refresh reads each row and writes it back before the deadline
beats.text: The controller issues REFRESH commands that open rows in turn, let the sense amps restore full charge, and close them again. While a bank refreshes it cannot serve reads, so refresh costs bandwidth and power.

beats.caption: Heat shortens retention, so hot memory refreshes twice as often
beats.text: Leakage roughly doubles every 10 C or so. Above 85 C the DDR rules halve the window to 32 ms, doubling refresh overhead. Dense AI servers run memory hot, so retention drives both lost bandwidth and DRAM design. Related: Micron (MU), SK hynix (000660.KS), Samsung (005930.KS).
